Electrical panel constraint modeling was added to ResStock via OpenStudio-HPXML measures in 2025 to assess whether the existing panel has enough capacity or breaker space to accommodate new loads from an energy retrofit. For details on panel constraint modeling, refer to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide [1]. Advanced air sealing does not introduce new electrical loads or circuits, so it has no impact on the electrical panel. However, electrical panel metrics are included as a standard output for this and all other envelope measures. Any panel constraints appearing in the upgrade results reflect pre-existing conditions, as this measure does not worsen them.

## 3.1  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview

The ResStock building stock energy model contains conditional probability distributions of building characteristics that are representative of the contiguous U.S. residential building stock. These are sampled to create a synthetic stock where each sample has an assigned option for each characteristic for each dwelling unit to be simulated. ResStock utilizes the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow to translate these dwelling characteristics into building models ready to be simulated via OpenStudio ® and EnergyPlus ® through the use of an HPXML file. For reference, the state of the OpenStudio-HPXML repository when the ResStock 2024 Release 2 dataset was created can be found here. Assumptions about the infiltration upgrades that are not explicitly defined in ResStock are taken care of in the BuildResidentialHPXML measure.

## 3.2  Advanced Air Sealing

In ResStock, building characteristics are translated to OS-HPXML parameters using the options\_lookup.tsv file. Measure upgrades, such as infiltration, are modeled as changes to baseline building characteristics. This section outlines the technical details of how infiltration upgrades are implemented in the ResStock workflow.

## ResStock Inputs for the Advanced Air Sealing Upgrade

Table 6 summarizes the inputs associated with the infiltration upgrade (advanced air sealing) in ResStock. These inputs are passed to OS-HPXML to generate the corresponding HPXML files for the simulation. In cases where infiltration details (ACH50) are not explicitly defined in ResStock, default values (Table 6) are assigned by OS-HPXML based on building characteristics.

Table 6. ResStock Argument Values for Infiltration Options

| ResStock Argument                 | All ACH    | Calculated by OpenStudio-HPXML?   |
|-----------------------------------|------------|-----------------------------------|
| air_leakage_units                 | ACH        | No                                |
| air_leakage_house_pressure        | 50         | No                                |
| air_leakage_value                 | 2.5 to 50  | No                                |
| air_leakage_type                  | Unit Total | No                                |
| site_shielding_of_home            | Normal     | No                                |
| air_leakage_leakiness_description | Auto       | Yes                               |

## Default Inputs from OpenStudio-HPXML for Infiltration Upgrade

The ResStock inputs in the table above are sent to OS-HPXML. Any values that are not specified by ResStock are calculated using the defaults in the BuildResidentialHPXML OpenStudio measure based on building characteristics. These characteristics include the building ' s floor area, number of stories, vintage, ceiling height, duct locations, foundation type, and climate zone. Other characteristics include stack effect, indoor-outdoor temperature difference, wind speed, and more. In multifamily and attached buildings, OS-HPXML assumes that some air leakage occurs between units rather than solely to the outside. To account for this, the software adjusts total infiltration based on the portion of the building envelope that is exposed to the exterior. More details of the infiltration model and default values can be found in the Alberta Air Infiltration Model (AIM-2) [16].

## 4 Results

## 4.1  Single Model Results

This section analyzes three example dwelling units that received advanced air sealing upgrades. Prior to the upgrades, each unit had air leakage rate of 50 ACH50 (Unit 1), 25 ACH50 (Unit 2), and 6 ACH50 (Unit 3). The upgrade reduced air leakage to 5 ACH50 for all units. The units are in Hawai ' i (climate zone 1A), Texas (climate zone 3A), and Alaska (climate zone 8AK). These represent a range of climate conditions. The floor area, heating setpoint, and cooling setpoint of these three dwelling units are different, so baseline performance across units is not comparable. This section focuses solely on the percentage energy reduction achieved by the advanced air sealing. The modeled annual energy consumption of the three example dwelling units before and after advanced air sealing upgrades are described below.

Figure 3 shows that the advanced air sealing upgrade led to modeled site energy savings for the example dwelling unit in Hawai ' i (Climate Zone 1A), where cooling dominates total consumption. Cooling energy use (including cooling and fan/pumps) decreased from 38.0 MBtu to 27.5 MBtu, a 27.6% reduction. Heating-related end uses decreased from 0.08 million BTU to 0.01 million BTU, an 87.5%. This low amount of heating is expected in a warm, tropical climate where outdoor temperatures rarely fall below heating setpoints, and many homes either lack heating systems or use them infrequently. In Hawai ' i, 85% of homes do not have heating equipment [17]. Note that the site energy consumption and the change heating fans/pumps energy between the baseline and the upgrade in the dwelling unit are negligible.

## 4.3  Stock Energy Impacts

Out of 550,000 modeled units (i.e., the total number of units modeled in the ResStock 2025.1 dataset to represent the national building stock), 507,100 units are applicable for the advanced air sealing upgrade (92.2%). For the 507,100 applicable units, the total weighted baseline modeled site energy consumption is 3,140 TWh per year. After applying the air sealing upgrade, the total modeled site energy consumption was reduced to 2,632 TWh per year, a 16.2% reduction. Figure 8 shows that site energy savings from air sealing primarily come from heating and cooling related end uses, with 27.1% electricity heating savings (64.2 TWh), 29.9% natural gas heating savings (318 TWh), 7.8% electricity cooling savings (27.1 TWh), and 3.8% cooling fan and pump energy savings (2.18 GWh). Energy savings were observed only in heating and cooling, while other end uses like lighting and appliances remained unchanged. This is because air sealing improves building performance by reducing air leakage. Thus, its impact is confined to systems that respond to indoor temperature fluctuations.

Site energy savings in space heating is greater than cooling. This is because the temperature difference (ΔT) between the indoor and outdoor environment is typically much smaller during the cooling season than during the heating season. This is one of the reasons why heating loads are often greater than cooling loads. For example, on a hot summer day, an indoor temperature of 72°F and an outdoor temperature of 95°F represents a ΔT of 23°F. On a cold winter day, an indoor temperature of 72°F and outdoor temperature of 25°F results in a ΔT of 47°F , approximately double the magnitude. Since the energy lost due to infiltration is directly proportional to ΔT, due to the HVAC systems conditioning the infiltrating outdoor air to the indoor setpoints, heating seasons experience higher infiltration-driven losses. This pattern aligns with typical climate conditions across the United States, where most regions have higher heating degree days than cooling degree days. Therefore, the dominant share of energy savings from advanced air sealing upgrades is expected to occur during the heating season, particularly in colder climates with leakier building envelopes and extended periods of high ΔT.

## 5 Discussion

This study evaluates the energy impacts of an advanced air sealing upgrade that reduces infiltration to 5 ACH50 for eligible existing units (≥6 ACH50). Results show that modeled site energy savings scale with baseline infiltration level, building vintage, and climate zones. Units with higher initial leakage achieved the largest absolute energy savings. Units starting at 40 -50 ACH50 experienced the greatest reductions when tightened to 5 ACH50, while homes starting near 6 -10 ACH50 saw smaller savings. Leakier homes experience greater convective heat loss (winter) and sensible/latent heat gain (summer), so reducing infiltration has a larger marginal impact. Baseline energy trends (e.g., 40 ACH50 vs. 50 ACH50 groups) are likely driven by other correlated building characteristics such as floor area, vintage, HVAC type, and fuel mix rather than infiltration alone. However, the general relationship between leakage and savings holds across the stock.

Site energy savings also increase with climate severity. Colder climate zones (e.g., 5A, 6A, 7A) show the highest absolute and percentage reductions because the number of heating degree days are greater than cooling degree days. Winter temperature difference is larger than summer difference and heating seasons are longer than cooling seasons. For example, a winter condition of 70°F indoors and 20°F outdoors yields a 50°F difference, while a summer condition of 75°F indoors and 95°F outdoors yields a 20°F difference. Because infiltration loads scale with temperature difference, heating savings are greater than cooling. In warm climates (e.g., 1A), annual consumption is predominately cooling, while heating is minimal or absent. Air sealing still reduces cooling loads, but percentage savings are smaller because temperature difference is modest and cooling seasons are less extreme than cold-climate heating seasons. Lastly, older homes show both higher baseline consumption and greater savings. Pre-1960 buildings show higher infiltration levels and therefore benefit more from tightening to 5 ACH50. Newer homes, especially post-2000 construction, begin closer to modern code performance and therefore show smaller savings.

## Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit end-use load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An ' end-use savings shape ' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock ™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna (2025) [1]. Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project [2].

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: advanced air sealing upgrade.

The advanced air sealing upgrade demonstrated 16% modeled total site energy savings (508 TWh) for the U.S. residential building stock (see Figure 8 for details). These savings are primarily attributed to:

- 30% stock natural gas heating savings (318 TWh)
- 27% stock electricity heating savings (64 TWh)
- 9% stock electricity cooling savings (27 TWh).

result.content:
Air sealing is a method used to reduce the amount of unwanted air that leaks in and out of a building through small gaps, cracks, and openings in the walls, floors, ceilings, and around windows and doors. These leaks allow outside air to enter the home and conditioned air to escape, which can lead to higher energy bills, drafts, uneven temperatures, indoor air quality concerns, and moisture issues [3], [4]. Studies show that air leakage can account for up to 30% of a home's heating and cooling costs [5]. By sealing these gaps, air sealing helps lower energy use, improves comfort by reducing drafts, supports better indoor air quality by keeping pollutants and allergens out, and protects the building's structure by reducing moisture intrusion [4]. Common air sealing techniques include: weatherstripping around doors and operable windows; caulking around stationary components such as window frames, baseboards, and wall penetrations; foam sealants or spray foam for larger gaps around plumbing penetrations, recessed lighting, and attic hatches; and airtight electrical boxes or gaskets around outlets and switches [3], [6]. ## 3 Modeling Approach

This section details how the upgrade measure is functionally modeled via ResStock into OpenStudio-HPXML. ResStock models residential air infiltration values expressed as ACH50. Each dwelling unit in the ResStock dataset is assigned an existing ACH50 value based on housing stock characteristics, informed by the Residential Diagnostics Database (ResDB). ResStock integrates this information using probabilistic sampling logic to represent the diversity of the U.S. housing stock. These infiltration rates are dependent on climate zone, floor area, and vintage. In ResStock, the current infiltration values are based on single-family detached blower door tests in units of ACH50. For single-family detached homes, the ACH50 values reflect total leakage to the outdoors, and buffer zones such as unconditioned attics, crawlspaces, and garages. However, for multifamily and single-family attached units, ResStock models leakage as total unit air leakage, which includes airflow to both the exterior and adjacent units. To estimate only the leakage to the exterior, the model scales the total sampled ACH50 by the ratio of the exterior-facing envelope area to the total envelope area. This adjusted exterior-only infiltration rate is then used in the simulation outputs.

 1. Group IECC zones into bins (1 -2, 3 -5, 6 -8) following IECC recommendations (Table 2).
 
 Average post-retrofit ACH50 values by climate zone bin using results from empirical studies in
 
 ## 2. Table 3.
 
 Identify the minimum observed infiltration reduction across studies,
 
 3. Table 3 (found 20%).
 4. Apply this minimum improvement to the 5 ACH50 target (from empirical data) to establish a qualifying threshold for existing buildings.
 
 The existing building 's infiltration, when reduced by 20%, should be 5 ACH50. This yields a minimum pre-upgrade value of 6.25 ACH50, but since ResStock models infiltration in whole numbers, 6 ACH50 is used instead. This reflects a 17% reduction. This is still supported by empirical studies that show achievable reductions from 6 to 4.8 ACH50 [13] and from 6.1 to 3.2 ACH50 [14]. Table 4 summarizes the applicable logic for the advanced air sealing used in this upgrade, and Table 5 presents the combined logic. Note that stock saturation is the percentage of dwellings in the building stock that this upgrade would apply to.

 Table 5. Combined Apply Logic for Advanced Air Sealing
 
 | Climate Zone   | Infiltration   | Target Infiltration   | Stock Saturation   |

 ## 3 Modeling Approach
 
 This section details how the upgrade measure is functionally modeled via ResStock into OpenStudio-HPXML. ResStock models residential air infiltration values expressed as ACH50. Each dwelling unit in the ResStock dataset is assigned an existing ACH50 value based on housing stock characteristics, informed by the Residential Diagnostics Database (ResDB). ResStock integrates this information using probabilistic sampling logic to represent the diversity of the U.S. housing stock. These infiltration rates are dependent on climate zone, floor area, and vintage. In ResStock, the current infiltration values are based on single-family detached blower door tests in units of ACH50. For single-family detached homes, the ACH50 values reflect total leakage to the outdoors, and buffer zones such as unconditioned attics, crawlspaces, and garages. However, for multifamily and single-family attached units, ResStock models leakage as total unit air leakage, which includes airflow to both the exterior and adjacent units. To estimate only the leakage to the exterior, the model scales the total sampled ACH50 by the ratio of the exterior-facing envelope area to the total envelope area. This adjusted exterior-only infiltration rate is then used in the simulation outputs.

 In this work, b uildings with infiltration rates ≥6 ACH 50 are eligible for an upgrade to 5 ACH50. This threshold serves as a nationally consistent benchmark across the housing stock. In practice, some new construction households in climate zones (e.g., climate zones 3 -5) require tighter envelopes such as 3 ACH50 or better (Table 2), and many older or leakier homes may only feasibly reach ~5 ACH50 through air sealing (Table 3). In practice, this infiltration level is typically achieved through blower-door-guided air sealing of attics, crawlspaces, rim joists, and other leakage pathways. Previous studies have shown that such practices can bring homes that start above 6 ACH50 down to or below the 5 ACH50 threshold [7] [13]. Therefore, 5 ACH50 provides a balanced and conservative target that represents a meaningful improvement for existing homes, while still allowing comparability across climate zones and building types.

 Electrical panel constraint modeling was added to ResStock via OpenStudio-HPXML measures in 2025 to assess whether the existing panel has enough capacity or breaker space to accommodate new loads from an energy retrofit. For details on panel constraint modeling, refer to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide [1]. Advanced air sealing does not introduce new electrical loads or circuits, so it has no impact on the electrical panel. However, electrical panel metrics are included as a standard output for this and all other envelope measures. Any panel constraints appearing in the upgrade results reflect pre-existing conditions, as this measure does not worsen them.
 
 ## 3.1  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview
 
 The ResStock building stock energy model contains conditional probability distributions of building characteristics that are representative of the contiguous U.S. residential building stock. These are sampled to create a synthetic stock where each sample has an assigned option for each characteristic for each dwelling unit to be simulated. ResStock utilizes the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow to translate these dwelling characteristics into building models ready to be simulated via OpenStudio ® and EnergyPlus ® through the use of an HPXML file. For reference, the state of the OpenStudio-HPXML repository when the ResStock 2024 Release 2 dataset was created can be found here. Assumptions about the infiltration upgrades that are not explicitly defined in ResStock are taken care of in the BuildResidentialHPXML measure.
 
 ## 3.2  Advanced Air Sealing
 
 In ResStock, building characteristics are translated to OS-HPXML parameters using the options\_lookup.tsv file. Measure upgrades, such as infiltration, are modeled as changes to baseline building characteristics. This section outlines the technical details of how infiltration upgrades are implemented in the ResStock workflow.
 
 ## ResStock Inputs for the Advanced Air Sealing Upgrade
 
 Table 6 summarizes the inputs associated with the infiltration upgrade (advanced air sealing) in ResStock. These inputs are passed to OS-HPXML to generate the corresponding HPXML files for the simulation. In cases where infiltration details (ACH50) are not explicitly defined in ResStock, default values (Table 6) are assigned by OS-HPXML based on building characteristics.

## Default Inputs from OpenStudio-HPXML for Infiltration Upgrade

The ResStock inputs in the table above are sent to OS-HPXML. Any values that are not specified by ResStock are calculated using the defaults in the BuildResidentialHPXML OpenStudio measure based on building characteristics. These characteristics include the building ' s floor area, number of stories, vintage, ceiling height, duct locations, foundation type, and climate zone. Other characteristics include stack effect, indoor-outdoor temperature difference, wind speed, and more. In multifamily and attached buildings, OS-HPXML assumes that some air leakage occurs between units rather than solely to the outside. To account for this, the software adjusts total infiltration based on the portion of the building envelope that is exposed to the exterior. More details of the infiltration model and default values can be found in the Alberta Air Infiltration Model (AIM-2) [16].

## 4 Results

## 4.1  Single Model Results

This section analyzes three example dwelling units that received advanced air sealing upgrades. Prior to the upgrades, each unit had air leakage rate of 50 ACH50 (Unit 1), 25 ACH50 (Unit 2), and 6 ACH50 (Unit 3). The upgrade reduced air leakage to 5 ACH50 for all units. The units are in Hawai ' i (climate zone 1A), Texas (climate zone 3A), and Alaska (climate zone 8AK). These represent a range of climate conditions. The floor area, heating setpoint, and cooling setpoint of these three dwelling units are different, so baseline performance across units is not comparable. This section focuses solely on the percentage energy reduction achieved by the advanced air sealing. The modeled annual energy consumption of the three example dwelling units before and after advanced air sealing upgrades are described below.

Figure 3 shows that the advanced air sealing upgrade led to modeled site energy savings for the example dwelling unit in Hawai ' i (Climate Zone 1A), where cooling dominates total consumption. Cooling energy use (including cooling and fan/pumps) decreased from 38.0 MBtu to 27.5 MBtu, a 27.6% reduction. Heating-related end uses decreased from 0.08 million BTU to 0.01 million BTU, an 87.5%. This low amount of heating is expected in a warm, tropical climate where outdoor temperatures rarely fall below heating setpoints, and many homes either lack heating systems or use them infrequently. In Hawai ' i, 85% of homes do not have heating equipment [17]. Note that the site energy consumption and the change heating fans/pumps energy between the baseline and the upgrade in the dwelling unit are negligible.

data.content:
In **ResStock 2025 Release 1** (Measure 11: *Advanced Air Sealing*, NLR/TP-5500-96738):

- **Eligibility:** Existing dwelling units across all climate zones with a baseline infiltration rate of **$\ge$ 6 ACH50** (air changes per hour at 50 Pascals). New construction and existing units below 6 ACH50 are excluded.
- **Target Leakage Level:** Eligible homes are sealed to **5.0 ACH50** (derived from a ~20% minimum empirical reduction rounded to whole-number baseline ACH50 bins, yielding at least a 17% reduction from 6 to 5 ACH50).
- **Share of Dwelling Units:** It applies to **92.2%** of existing baseline dwelling units (excluding the remaining **7.8%**).
